newsitem.title: SPAIN: Captivity ends for two held by Basque guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Captivity ends for two held by Basque guerrillas.

text.p: A Spanish businessman was released by Basque separatist rebels on Tuesday after his family paid nearly $7 million in ransom, and a second hostage was rescued by police from a tiny cell in which he was held "like a beast", officials said.
In a fast-moving series of events, police tracked down and arrested four suspected members of the ETA guerrilla group who were believed to have been holding the prisoners.
Businessman Cosme Delclaux, an ETA prisoner for the past 232 days, was found drugged and tied to a tree near Bilbao just after midnight.
His family had paid his captors $6.8 million, the largest ransom obtained by ETA, and agreed in secret negotiations to hand over another $3.4 million after his release, police sources said.
Only hours later, an elite police unit found ETA's longest-held captive, prison worker Jose Antonio Ortega Lara, in a tiny cell beneath a warehouse near the Basque town of Mondragon.

The Spanish government hailed the rescue and arrests as a double blow against the separatist group, which has waged a violent 29-year struggle for an independent Basque homeland. The group has kidnapped 76 people since 1970, of whom 68 survived the ordeal.

"This is a very happy day, but the government knows it still has a hard and difficult task ahead," Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar told a news conference. "We are not going to change our anti-terrorist policy".
But some officials said the ransom payment for Delclaux's release set a damaging precedent and could embolden ETA to take even more hostages.

Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said it was a "complete coincidence" that Declaux had been released on the same night as Ortega Lara. An operation to free the prison worker had been in the works for some months, he added.
Authorities said Delclaux, 34, was found following an anonymous phone call to a newspaper with links to ETA.

He had been left tied to a tree about 25 km (15 miles) from Bilbao, near Elorrio in the Basque province of Vizcaya. Officials said he was disoriented, apparently as a result of being given some type of sedative, but was in good health.
Police later arrested four suspected rebels in their homes and took them to an abandoned industrial site near Mondragon where authorities believed Ortega Lara was being held, Mayor Oreja said.
But the four refused to aid police in freeing the prison worker and officers had to untangle a sophisticated hydraulic system to access his cell which took almost two hours.
"They didn't cooperate at all ... if police hadn't found him, they intended to let him starve to death," said Mayor Oreja.
Mayor Oreja said police had located the area where Ortega Lara was being held some weeks ago. He had been held captive for 532 days in a cell in which he could scarcely stand.
"ETA treated their prisoners like beasts, but it's clear that the beasts are them," said Mayor Oreja.

Ortega Lara appeared in good health but had lost a lot of weight after being fed only fruit and vegetables. He was taken to a hospital in San Sebastian for an examination and then returned to his home in Burgos, where he was greeted by hordes of cheering supporters lining the streets.
The two kidnappings had sparked a national outcry.

Ortega Lara was abducted from the northern Spanish town of Burgos on January 17, 1996. ETA said it kidnapped him to put pressure on the government to end what it termed the repression of Basque political prisoners.
Delclaux, a lawyer and the son of a wealthy Basque industrialist, was kidnapped on his way home from work as a consultant at a multimedia firm in a Vizcaya technological park on November 11, 1996.
In recent weeks, his family was reported to have received a package containing two bullets, interpreted as a threat to execute him unless payment was made.
